meta.title: Who really said "So I'm Ugly. So What? I Never Saw Anyone Hit with His Face"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Yogi Berra really said it. First documented in Milton Gross's 1948 book Yankee Doodles, though in different words. The tidy one-liner is a later compression.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'So I'm Ugly. So What? I Never Saw Anyone Hit with His Face'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Berra, documented in print from 1948 — but the neat modern wording is a compression of what he actually said. The full citation trail, side by side.

answer.label: Spoken by

answer.sourceLine: The quip is genuinely his. The earliest printing Quote Investigator documents is the Berra chapter of sportswriter Milton Gross’s 1948 book Yankee Doodles, and Berra printed it himself in The Yogi Book (1998) and When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It! (copyright 2001). Only the neat modern wording is new — the closing clause is his word for word, but the punchy “So I’m ugly. So what?” opener replaces the set-up he actually used.

source.excerpt: When they remind him that he’s ugly, Yogi has a pat answer. “It don’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball and I never saw anybody hit one with his face.”
trail: 1948 — the earliest documented printing. Sportswriter Milton Gross gave Berra a chapter in Yankee Doodles, his collection of New York Yankee profiles, and recorded the reply Berra kept ready for teammates who called him ugly: all you have to do is hit the ball, and he never saw anybody hit one with his face. Quote Investigator verified the page on paper ↗

The book is real and datable. An independent catalog record confirms Gross’s Yankee Doodles as a 245-page volume published in Boston by House of Kent Pub. Co. in 1948 — so the cited quote page falls well inside it. Open Library edition record ↗

1949–1955 — it spreads, and the words move. Collier’s Weekly printed “I never saw nobody hit one with his face”; an Associated Press profile in 1952 and Grantland Rice’s column in 1953 each carried their own variant; and The American Mercury in 1955 traced the retort back to bench-jockeying from Birdie Tebbetts. The citations are laid out in order ↗

1998 and 2001 — Berra claims it himself. He gives the short form in The Yogi Book, the book he assembled specifically to sort what he had said from what he hadn’t, and the fuller version in When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It! The Yogi Book is digitized at the Internet Archive ↗

source.rightsNote: Berra’s own retellings are plainly in copyright — The Yogi Book (Workman, 1998) and When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It! (Hyperion, copyright 2001). For the 1948 first printing, Milton Gross’s Yankee Doodles, we have not established whether the US copyright was renewed, so we have not established that it entered the public domain either — treat the line as in copyright. Quoting the sentence with attribution is ordinary fair comment; reproducing the surrounding pages is not.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.heading: Who was Yogi Berra?
author.metaLine: 1925–2015 · Hall of Fame catcher, New York Yankees
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra caught for the New York Yankees from 1946 to 1963 and played a last season with the Mets in 1965, winning ten World Series titles as a player, three American League MVP awards and eighteen All-Star selections before his election to the Hall of Fame in 1972. He ended up at least as famous for his talk as for his catching — and famous enough that lines he had never said were routinely handed to him, which is why he called one of his own books The Yogi Book: I really didn’t say everything I said!

presentation.verifiedQuote: It don’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball and I never saw anybody hit one with his face.

copyAttribution: “It don’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball and I never saw anybody hit one with his face.” —Yogi Berra, quoted in Milton Gross, Yankee Doodles (Boston: House of Kent Publishing Co., 1948), 115. The tidy modern form now in circulation, “So I’m ugly. So what? I never saw anyone hit with his face,” is a later compression of this; its closing clause matches Berra’s own wording in When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It! (Hyperion, copyright 2001), 112.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the version you’ve seen
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this line, and the attribution to Berra is sound. What has drifted is the wording — which matters here, because the sentence everyone quotes is not the sentence anyone recorded.

items.why: “So I’m ugly. So what? I never saw anyone hit with his face” is the form that circulates in quotation books and on quote sites — it is the version a reader brought to Quote Investigator in the first place — but it matches none of the printings from 1948 to 2001. The second half is Berra’s exactly; the “So I’m ugly. So what?” opener stands in for his real set-up, “It doesn’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball.” Quote Investigator sets the wordings side by side ↗

Retellings usually stage this as one squelch delivered once. Both Berra and the man who first printed it describe a habit instead: Gross in 1948 called it Berra’s “pat answer” to teammates who reminded him he was ugly, and Berra in 2001 called it his “stock answer” whenever he was asked about his looks. Both passages are quoted in full at Quote Investigator ↗

Berra is one of the most quote-magnetised names in American life — enough that he titled a book I really didn’t say everything I said!, and enough that biographer Allen Barra argues a “pseudo-Yogi” was manufactured around him, largely by his friend Joe Garagiola. That is precisely why a line this good deserves a source rather than a shrug. Slate on the invented Yogi ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is Berra’s and it was in print by 1948 — but the version you have probably seen is a later tightening of the words he actually used. See the full citation trail at Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why the line existed at all
lead: Berra came up into a clubhouse and a league full of bench jockeys who had decided his face was the joke. The American Mercury later reported that Birdie Tebbetts got it going by hollering across at him, “Hey, Berra, how does your wife like living in a tree?” — after which opposing players spent a season swinging from dugout roofs and bellowing like Tarzan. By that account it took Berra all season to think up his answer. Quote Investigator reproduces the Mercury anecdote ↗

Knowing the real wording changes what the line is. The version in circulation is a wisecrack. What Gross wrote down in 1948 is a working man’s argument — it doesn’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket, all you have to do is hit the ball — with the face joke as the closing move. Berra treated it as equipment rather than a one-off: Gross called it his “pat answer,” and Berra himself later called it his “stock answer” when people asked about his looks.
context.detailsSummary: Every wording we can document, in order
detailsBody: 1948 · Milton Gross, Yankee Doodles: “It don’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball and I never saw anybody hit one with his face.”
1949 · Collier’s Weekly: “It don’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket … All you gotta do is hit the ball, and I never saw nobody hit one with his face.”
1952 · Associated Press: “It don’t matter what they say. All you have to do in this racket is to hit the ball. I never saw anybody hit one with his face.”
1953 · Grantland Rice: “You don’t hit with your face.”

1960 · Frank Litsky, The Milwaukee Sentinel American Weekly: “But it don’t bother me. I never yet saw anybody hit the baseball with their face. Besides, I like to get kidded; that means they like me. When they stop kidding me, I’m in trouble.”
1998 · Berra, The Yogi Book: “So? I don’t hit with my face.”
2001 · Berra, When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It!: “It doesn’t matter if you’re ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball, and I never saw anyone hit with his face.”

All but the 1960 newspaper wording are transcribed in order at Quote Investigator ↗, which does not cite it; that one is sourced at Wikiquote ↗ — and none of them is the sentence people usually quote.

schema.claimReviewed: Yogi Berra originated the “never saw anyone hit with his face” retort about his looks, popularly quoted as “So I’m ugly. So what? I never saw anyone hit with his face.” — a later compression of the wording documented from 1948 on.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Yogi Berra did create and use this riposte, with good evidence starting in 1948; earliest citation is Milton Gross, Yankee Doodles, chapter 'Beauty's Only Skin Deep', quote page 115, House of Kent Publishing Company, Boston, 1948 (verified on paper), reading 'It don't matter if you're ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball and I never saw anybody hit one with his face.' Also transcribes Collier's Weekly (13 Aug 1949, Gordon Manning), Telegraph-Herald AP article (27 Jan 1952, Murray Rose), Grantland Rice (Reading Eagle, 19 Mar 1953), The American Mercury (Oct 1955, Birdie Tebbetts 'living in a tree' anecdote), The Yogi Book (Workman, 1998, p.112: 'So? I don't hit with my face.') and When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It! (Hyperion, copyright 2001, p.112: 'It doesn't matter if you're ugly in this racket. All you have to do is hit the ball, and I never saw anyone hit with his face.'). The compact form 'So I'm ugly. So what? I never saw anyone hit with his face' is the version presented by the questioner and matches none of the documented printings.

Yogi Berra, full name Lawrence Peter Berra, born 12 May 1925 in St. Louis, died 22 September 2015; catcher for the New York Yankees 1946-1963 and the New York Mets in 1965; 10 World Series championships as a player, 18 All-Star selections, 3 AL MVP awards, Hall of Fame induction 1972; famous for 'Yogi-isms' and for saying 'I really didn't say everything I said' about quotes falsely attributed to him.
Open Library edition record for Yankee Doodles by Milton Gross: published 1948 by House of Kent Pub. Co., Boston, 245 pages.
Internet Archive holds a digitized copy of 'The Yogi book: I really didn't say everything I said!' by Yogi Berra (1925-2015), published 1998 by Workman Publishing, New York, 127 pages.

Wikiquote's Yogi Berra page carries a 1960 wording of this same retort in its main Sourced quotes section (not Disputed or Misattributed): 'But it don't bother me. I never yet saw anybody hit the baseball with their face. Besides, I like to get kidded; that means they like me. When they stop kidding me, I'm in trouble.' — cited to Frank Litsky, 'Stupid, You Say?', The Milwaukee Sentinel American Weekly (Sunday, 18 September 1960), p. 7. Quote Investigator's citation trail does not include this instance. The page does not carry the compressed modern form 'So I'm ugly. So what? I never saw anyone hit with his face'; it does carry 'I really didn't say everything I said' as a sourced Yogi-ism and documents other Berra attributions that post-date the sayings themselves.

Slate reports that many Yogi-isms were invented or amplified, quoting biographer Allen Barra that Joe Garagiola 'built his whole career on these Yogi-isms, many of which were made-up' and that Garagiola 'created a pseudo-Yogi that took on a life of its own'; also cites Berra's 'I really didn't say everything I said.' The article does not mention the ugly/hit-with-his-face quip.
Milton Gross (1912-1973) was a New York Post sportswriter who covered the New York Yankees beat and wrote Yankee Doodles, a 1948 book about the team.
